status: Choose and configure each library against its installed-version documentation.
instruction: Select an optional tool only when the application's requirements match its use case. Explain the selection, check compatibility with the project's lockfile, and follow its installed-version documentation. Do not install the whole menu.

items.when: Users need to sign in with Google, GitHub, Apple or an OpenID Connect provider.
items.use: Integrate provider authentication with the application's existing accounts and sessions.
items.boundary: Account linking, session management and permissions remain application concerns. SAML is a separate requirement.

items.when: Login attempts, API calls, uploads or expensive actions need limits.
items.use: Define limits by actor, operation and time window; choose a backend that matches the deployment.
items.boundary: A node-local counter does not automatically enforce a cluster-wide quota. Choose the algorithm's burst behavior deliberately.

items.when: Features need gradual rollout, per-customer access or an operational off switch.
items.use: Choose an Ecto or Redis persistence adapter and configure synchronization between nodes.
items.boundary: Keep permission checks separate from rollout flags. Remove expired flags and restrict the management interface.

items.when: Uploads need to live in an S3 or compatible object store.
items.use: Use ExAws with its S3 service module for object operations and signed URLs. In a LiveView app, connect it to the upload flow.
items.boundary: The storage service, credentials, access rules and lifecycle policy are separate. Check which operations a compatible service actually supports.

items.when: The product needs thumbnails, resized uploads, image conversion or watermarks.
items.use: Process images through the libvips-backed Image API; use Oban for work that needs retries.
items.boundary: Vix/libvips introduces native runtime requirements. Check the deployment target and required codecs, and limit input dimensions and processing work.

items.when: Invoices, reports or other HTML documents need downloadable PDFs.
items.use: Render application-owned HTML and CSS through a managed Chrome process.
items.boundary: Chrome is an additional runtime dependency; PDF/A conversion also uses Ghostscript. Isolate rendering and control access to external resources.

items.when: Users need bulk uploads, data exports or integrations through CSV files.
items.use: Parse and write streams; validate each imported row through the application's business rules.
items.boundary: CSV parsing does not validate field types or business rules. Define malformed-row handling and spreadsheet formula escaping for exports.

items.when: External consumers need an OpenAPI contract for the Phoenix API.
items.use: Describe operations and schemas, validate requests, and test responses against the specification.
items.boundary: A schema does not enforce ownership or authorization. Keep the published contract aligned with application behavior.

items.when: Clients specifically need GraphQL queries, mutations or subscriptions.
items.use: Expose the existing business layer through a schema; use Dataloader where batching is needed.
items.boundary: Resolvers still need authorization and query-cost limits. Ordinary JSON endpoints remain simpler when GraphQL adds no client benefit.

items.when: Chat, collaborative screens or live rooms need connected-user state.
items.use: Track presence metadata and broadcast joins and leaves through Phoenix's existing realtime infrastructure.
items.boundary: Presence is ephemeral and eventually consistent. It is not a durable audit trail, access-control system or editing-conflict resolver.

items.when: The application needs interface copy in multiple languages.
items.use: Use the Gettext integration already present in typical Phoenix projects; maintain translation catalogs and plural forms.
items.boundary: It does not translate user-authored content automatically. Dates, amounts and units need locale-aware formatting too.

items.when: Dates, numbers, currencies and units must follow the user's locale.
items.use: Use CLDR-based formatting and parsing. For new projects, evaluate Localize as the documented successor to the ex_cldr family.
items.boundary: Existing ex_cldr applications need a planned migration. Check runtime requirements and package locale data for deployment.

items.when: Prices, invoices or balances need explicit currencies and decimal arithmetic.
items.use: Represent amount and currency together and make rounding rules explicit.
items.boundary: This is not payment processing, tax calculation or an accounting ledger. The package is ex_money; check its major-version migration notes.

items.when: The product needs text generation, streamed responses or model tool calls through hosted APIs.
items.use: Use a common Elixir interface to supported model providers and keep provider-specific settings explicit.
items.boundary: Provider capabilities differ. The client does not supply evaluation, permission checks or a reliable autonomous workflow; test the exact model and features used.

items.when: The application needs stateful agents that select or coordinate steps, react to signals or run under OTP supervision.
items.use: Model the system with agents, actions, signals and directives, and run long-lived agents through Jido's supervised runtime.
items.boundary: Jido is an application architecture, not an LLM client. Prefer a plain GenServer, an Oban workflow or an explicit function pipeline when the behavior is fixed and simple.

items.when: A language model must select tools, keep agent state or run a bounded multistep reasoning loop.
items.use: Add Jido.AI to a Jido agent and use ReqLLM for provider access. Define tools as actions, and keep model selection, timeouts and tool policy explicit.
items.boundary: Model output is untrusted and nondeterministic. Restrict tool permissions and side effects, set cost and step limits, require approval for high-risk operations, and test representative tasks.

items.when: Embeddings are useful for semantic retrieval or recommendations alongside existing PostgreSQL data.
items.use: Enable the PostgreSQL vector extension and use the Elixir pgvector integration with Ecto or Postgrex.
items.boundary: The library does not generate embeddings. Verify database-extension support, dimensions, indexes and retrieval quality against representative queries.

items.when: Inference should run on infrastructure you control, using a supported pretrained model.
items.use: Load supported model architectures with Bumblebee and serve predictions through Nx.Serving.
items.boundary: Plan model memory, a suitable numerical backend and hardware. Model compatibility and licensing need to be checked individually.

items.when: The application consumes a stream from Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS or another supported source.
items.use: Build concurrent processing stages with batching, acknowledgements and back-pressure.
items.boundary: The source connector determines delivery behavior. Keep handlers safe to retry; ordinary application jobs still fit Oban.

items.when: Imports, analytics or reports need dataframe transformations over CSV, Parquet or similar datasets.
items.use: Use typed series and dataframes for grouping, joining and transforming tabular data.
items.boundary: The default Polars backend uses native code. Check deployment support and memory use; routine application queries still belong in Ecto.

items.when: Resources, actions, policies and derived APIs form a substantial part of the application.
items.use: Evaluate Ash early as the domain layer beneath Phoenix, with only the extensions the product needs.
items.boundary: This changes how business logic is modeled. It is an architectural choice, not a small utility to install beside an unchanged contexts design.
